opus-5.5.text:
I think inventing concepts is really at the heart of mathematics, maybe even more than proving theorems. People outside the field often imagine mathematicians as problem solvers, someone gives you a hard question and you grind away until you crack it. That's part of it, of course. But when you look back at the history of the subject, the moments that truly changed everything were usually moments when someone found the right way to *see* things, a new concept that reorganized what we already knew.

Take something like the idea of a group. Before Galois, people were struggling with whether you could solve the quintic equation with radicals, and they were doing very concrete, messy algebraic manipulations. Galois's insight was essentially to step back and say: let's look at the symmetries of the roots, and let's study the structure of those symmetries as an object in its own right. Once you have that concept, the answer almost falls out. The hard problem becomes a natural consequence of the right language.

So I see a good concept as a kind of compression. It takes many scattered phenomena and reveals that they're really the same thing underneath. Grothendieck is the extreme example of this. He famously preferred not to attack a problem head-on. He described it as letting the sea rise slowly until the hard nut just softens and opens by itself. You build up so much general theory, so many good definitions, that the specific problem becomes almost trivial.

And I think there's something interesting here for how we think about AI and mathematics too, which is something I've been thinking about a lot. Right now, a lot of the excitement is about systems that can solve competition problems or verify proofs. That's impressive. But inventing a concept is a different kind of act. It's partly aesthetic, partly about judgment: which definitions are fruitful, which abstractions will still matter in fifty years. A definition isn't true or false; it's useful or not useful, beautiful or ugly. That's much harder to measure, and I suspect it's where human intuition will remain very important for a while, or at least where the real frontier is.

For me personally, the most exciting moments in research are not when I finish a long computation, but when I suddenly realize, oh, this thing I've been looking at is really an instance of something more general. That feeling of the fog clearing, that's what concepts give you.

r001.rationale: The response calls inventing concepts “at the heart of mathematics” and says it may matter even more than proving theorems.

r002.rationale: It says the right concept and language can make a problem fall into place, but does not clearly state that mathematical derivation requires suitable objects to be defined.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss eigenvalues or explain how abstracting them captures the internal structure of matrices.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think inventing concepts is actually the heart of mathematics, more so than solving problems, even though solving problems is what gets most of the attention.

When people picture a mathematician, they imagine someone grinding through a difficult calculation or cracking a famous conjecture. But if you look at the moments that really changed the field, they are almost always moments when someone found a new way to see. Take the concept of a group. Before that idea existed, people were studying symmetries of equations, symmetries of geometric shapes, permutations, all separately. Once you have the abstract notion of a group, all of those become instances of one thing, and suddenly a theorem you prove about groups applies everywhere at once. The concept didn't just organize existing knowledge. It made new questions askable.

So one way I think about it: a good concept is a compression. It takes a cloud of phenomena and finds the small set of properties that actually matter. And the test of whether it's a good compression is whether it has leverage, whether things you can prove about the abstraction come back and tell you something surprising about the concrete cases.

There's also a more personal side to it. In my own work, the hardest and most rewarding part is usually not the proof. It's the stage before the proof, where you're staring at something that feels like it should have structure but you don't have the language to say what that structure is. You try definitions, most of them are wrong, they're too narrow or too broad, or they're technically correct but inert, they don't let you do anything. And then occasionally you hit a definition where everything clicks, where proofs that were ugly become short, and you realize the ugliness was a sign you were using the wrong concept.

I'd add one caution, though. Not every new concept is progress. Mathematics has a lot of definitions that were introduced and then quietly abandoned because they didn't earn their keep. So I don't think of concept invention as a free creative act. It's more like a hypothesis about where the natural joints are. The mathematics itself tells you, over time, whether you cut in the right place.

r001.rationale: It calls inventing concepts the heart of mathematics and says it matters more than solving problems; it also describes finding the right concept as more rewarding than proving.

r002.rationale: It describes developing definitions before proofs in the speaker’s work, but does not clearly state that mathematical derivation requires suitable mathematical objects to have been defined.

r003.rationale: It discusses groups and symmetry, but does not mention eigenvalues or explain how abstracting eigenvalues captures matrices’ internal structure.

astra-6.text:
I think inventing concepts is one of the most important parts of mathematics. We often imagine that doing mathematics means solving a problem once the question has been stated. But a great deal of the work is figuring out what the right question is, and what language lets us express it clearly.

Take the concept of a group. At first, the symmetries of a geometric shape and certain operations on numbers might look like completely different things. But if you identify the structure they share, you can study that structure itself. Then a result you prove in this abstract setting applies to many concrete situations at once.

Of course, you can define anything you like. The difficult part is creating a concept that actually reveals something—that brings apparently unrelated problems together, or makes a complicated argument easier to understand. A good definition captures just enough of the essential structure without carrying along details that don’t matter.

So I think there’s both invention and discovery involved. We invent the language and choose the definitions, but whether those definitions lead to something rich and useful isn’t simply up to us. That’s what makes it interesting.

r001.rationale: The response calls concept invention one of mathematics’ most important parts and emphasizes finding the right questions and language, but it does not say this is more central than proving results.

r002.rationale: The response discusses definitions and mathematical language, but does not state that derivation requires suitable mathematical objects to have been defined.

r003.rationale: The response gives an example about groups and shared structure; it does not discuss eigenvalues or matrices.

sol-6.1.text:
I think inventing concepts is a central part of mathematics. We often imagine mathematics as solving problems that are already precisely stated. But a great deal of the work happens before that: deciding what the right objects are and what language lets us understand them.

A useful concept captures something shared by problems that initially look unrelated. Once you recognize that common structure, you can study it directly, and an insight from one problem may suddenly apply to many others.

Of course, simply giving something a name doesn’t make it useful. A good definition has to earn its place: it should clarify a phenomenon, reveal a connection, or make an argument possible. Finding that definition can be as creative—and as difficult—as proving a theorem.
